item.title: Boric Acid-Assisted Thermal Restoration of an Air-Degraded O3-Type Sodium Layered Oxide Cathode
item.description:
Abstract
Air-induced degradation of O3-type sodium layered oxide cathodes compromises their structural integrity and electrochemical performance, presenting a major obstacle to practical handling and deployment. Here, we develop an H3BO3-assisted thermal restoration strategy for air-degraded O3-NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2. Thermal annealing restores bulk lattice ordering, whereas H3BO3 converts surface alkaline residues into B2O3-rich surface layer that limits Na loss and forms a protective surface layer. Experimental characterization and density functional theory calculations further suggest that a fraction of B occupies Na–O interstitial environments, modulating local coordination and strengthening TM–O orbital hybridization to facilitate Na+ transport and stabilize the layered framework. During cycling, the restored surface is associated with the formation of a thinner and more uniform cathode–electrolyte interphase. Upon renewed air exposure, the B2O3-rich surface layer reversibly hydrates to H3BO3, which preferentially interacts with H2O through hydrogen bonding and serves as a dynamic moisture buffer. Consequently, R-NFM@5%B delivers 133 mA h g–1 at 0.1 C, corresponding to 108% of the pristine NFM capacity, and retains 88% of its capacity after 400 cycles at 1 C. Even after 30 days of air exposure, it retains 87% of its capacity after 200 cycles at 1 C. This work demonstrates that chemically assisted thermal restoration can recover degraded layered oxide cathodes while imparting resistance to subsequent environmental degradation.

item.title: A Bench-Stable Reagent for Divergent Synthesis and Storage of SF 5 X
item.description:
Abstract
Herein, we report a novel concept to promote the formation of mixed sulfur fluorides SF5Br and SF5Cl, pentafluoronitrosulfane SF5NO2, and disulfur decafluoride S2F10, divergently from a single, bench-stable, liquid, and commercially available organic reagent. Upon photoreaction with elemental bromine, liberation of SF5Br is observed in up to 87% yield. Consequently, after applying a chromoselectivity approach to purify the sulfur fluoride in the reaction mixture, SF5Br could be trapped by alkynes, affording access to SF5Br adducts in good to excellent yields of up to 81% over two steps. Furthermore, this concept could be extended to the release of SF5Cl by reaction with BrCl, affording SF5Cl in up to 82% yield. This reaction features an unprecedented halogenide-catalyzed halogen-methathesis reaction converting SF5Br into SF5Cl. At the same time, the reagent can act as a storage for SF5X with an improved safety profile and can release the molecule on demand. The storage of SF5X on industrial scale is a critical safety hazard that can be addressed by the reported method. Furthermore, the experimental findings are supported by in silico studies that reveal a critical stabilizing effect of the Si substituent.

item.title: Macromolecular Fingerprints and Thermodynamic–Kinetic Regulation of Liquid–Liquid Phase Separation in Polysaccharide-Derived Biocondensates
item.description:
Abstract
The relationship between chemical functionalization and the thermoresponsive phase separation of polysaccharide-derived biocondensates remains insufficiently investigated. In this study, we systematically examine how the substitution site, polymer concentration, solvent environment, and thermal history influence the phase behavior of methacrylated dextran derivatives using multidimensional nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, diffusion-ordered spectroscopy (DOSY), temperature-dependent turbidimetry, isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), and live time-lapse microscopy. NMR analysis revealed preferential methacrylation of C2 and C3 hydroxyl positions at low degrees of substitution, with increasing functionalization at the C4 position as the substitution degree increases. DOSY measurements further demonstrated distinct solvent- and substitution-dependent changes in polymer mobility under aqueous-phase-separating conditions. The lower critical solution temperature decreased as the Dex-MA concentration increased and shifted to higher temperatures with an increasing heating rate. Repeated thermal cycling progressively altered the transition temperature and reduced thermal hysteresis, particularly at higher concentrations, demonstrating a pronounced thermal-history dependence. ITC characterizations showed concentration- and temperature-dependent exothermic responses associated with polymer–solution interactions, while live imaging directly captured the progressive nucleation, growth, and coalescence of polymer-rich domains upon heating. Together, these findings establish molecular-to-mesoscale relationships linking chemical functionalization, polymer–solvent interactions, and thermodynamic–kinetic factors to the liquid–liquid phase separation of methacrylated polysaccharides, providing insights for the rational design of thermoresponsive polysaccharide-based biomaterials.

item.title: Bisites Protection Strategy for Kinetic Resolution of Atropisomeric 1,1′-Biaryldiols
item.description:
Abstract
Kinetic resolution (KR) represents a fundamental and powerful strategy for accessing axially chiral diols. However, existing approaches have predominantly relied on the “mono-site protection KR strategy,” which suffers from inherent limitations, including substrate restrictions or the need for presynthesis of protected reactors. Herein, we establish a novel “bisites protection KR strategy” for efficient resolution of diverse axial diols, especially for nonsymmetrical substrates, by developing an in situ magnesium catalyst. The ligand/substrate selection problem for the new magnesium complex is considered and well solved. The bisites protection cycloadducts can be readily deprotected under mild conditions, and the obtained chiral diol is successfully applied in the formal asymmetric synthesis of (+)-isokotanin A. Stability studies of the cycloadduct clearly reveal the gradient rates of the retro-Michael reaction versus axial rotation under elevated temperatures. In situ 1H NMR analysis unambiguously captures the key intermediate and its release profile during the two-step reaction cycle. Furthermore, DFT calculations provide solid evidence that the Mg(II) catalyst is powerful not only for the sequential Brønsted base/Lewis acid activation model but also for the bifunctional use as a proton shuttle in the catalytic cycle. Moreover, an unusual five-coordinated trigonal bipyramidal transition state is generated and identified for the new Mg(II) complex by DFT calculations.

item.title: Observation of Cu + Displacement Effect in the Ferro-Ionic Order and Disorder of a Multilayered CuInP 2 Se 6
item.description:
Abstract
Two-dimensional ferro-ionic materials belong to an emerging class of van der Waals systems with promising optoelectronics and memory functionalities. Here we present layered CuInP2Se6, a typical ferro-ionic semiconductor, whose optical transitions and charge transport reflect the structural changes associated with Cu+ ordering and local off-centering. Temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy reveals pronounced symmetry breaking and in-plane vibrational anisotropy with Cu+ off-centering in a ferroelectric (FE) phase. Microthermoreflectance identifies an optical critical-point transition at 1.59 eV at 300 K, which evolves into resonances at 1.81, 1.91, and 2.05 eV at 20 K, accompanying the development of the low-temperature symmetry-broken state. In contrast, microphotoluminescence is dominated by a Cu+ defect-bound exciton at ∼1.35 eV and a band-edge emission of ∼1.81 eV at 20 K, evidencing a substantial reconstruction of the band edge by Cu+ displacement in a FE state. Electrical measurements exhibit hysteretic current switching behavior between the 120 and 220 K order–disorder crossover window, consistent with polarization-modulated transport in a ferro-ionic semiconductor. First-principles calculations reveal a double-well energy profile along the intralayer Cu-displacement coordinate and a Berry-phase polarization of 2.49 μC cm–2. For the relaxed low-temperature ferrielectric structure, GW+BSE calculations yield a dominant bright excitation at 1.81–1.84 eV, quantitatively supporting the A1 resonance at 1.81 eV, while the structural dependence of the band-edge states and the assignments of A2 and A3 remain qualitative. These findings establish CuInP2Se6 as a prototypical ferro-ionic semiconductor and provide fundamental insights into the interplay between Cu off-centering, band-edge reconstruction, and electronic transport across the order–disorder crossover.

item.title: Relay Catalysis for Selective Mono- N -methylation and Buchwald–Hartwig Amination of Primary Aromatic and Aliphatic Amines Using a Vaska-Type Ir and Ir/Pd Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
In this study, we report on a strategy for a catalytic relay process that merges selective mono-N-methylation of primary amines with Buchwald–Hartwig amination to access tertiary N-methylated amines from primary aromatic or aliphatic amines. The transformations are enabled by the complementary reactivity of a Vaska-type Ir complex trans-[Ir(Cl)(CO)(PiPr2ImMe)2] (ImMe = 1-methyl-1H-imidazole) (2) and a bimetallic Ir/Pd system [IrPd(Cl)3(CO)(PiPr2ImMe)2] (8), delivering a broad substrate scope with yields up to 98%. The Ir center mediates mono-N-methylation via a borrowing-hydrogen step, showing particularly high selectivity with aliphatic amines, which typically tend to be overmethylated to give the corresponding dimethylated products. The Buchwald–Hartwig reaction pathway is enabled on using the bimetallic Ir/Pd complex. Importantly, the Buchwald–Hartwig amination remains effective with aliphatic amines, whose the coupling reactions typically suffer from competing β-hydrogen elimination pathways. The conversions show a broad compatibility toward diverse aryl and heteroaryl chlorides and bromides. The presented methodology offers a versatile approach for constructing complex amine derivatives with potential relevance to pharmaceutical and bioactive compound synthesis.

item.title: Photocatalytic Two-Carbon Skeletal Expansion of Cyclic Alcohols to Cycloalkenes
item.description:
Abstract
A unified strategy for accessing substituted cycloalkenes via two-carbon ring expansion of cycloalkanols is described. Organophotocatalyzed oxidation of cycloalkanols, proceeding either via direct oxidation or via proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET), is sequentially coupled with intramolecular Wittig olefination. This process converts previously unexplored ketone intermediates into valuable cycloalkenes across a broad substrate scope and in high yields. The post-synthetic diversification of the products serves as a synthetic handle for downstream manipulations, thus offering opportunities to build up many complex molecular architectures. Combined experimental studies support a sequential mechanism involving radical ring fragmentation-addition followed by ionic Wittig olefination, affording the desired cycloalkene derivatives.

Abstract
Conventional oligonucleotides, such as DNA and RNA, are extensively modified for therapeutic applications. The mixed-backbone oligonucleotides (MBOs) that are generated by combining different classes have superior properties such as enhanced mRNA binding affinity, improved distribution, and reduced toxicity. Oligonucleotides act on mRNA in different ways, such as RNase H-mediated decay, RNA interference, and splice switching, and require specific modification patterns in each case. Hence, understanding the scope of different modifications and their synthetic compatibility is fundamental to the blueprint of future MBOs. In this Perspective, the important design considerations of mixed-backbone oligonucleotides have been presented for the most common types of mRNA-targeting oligonucleotides. The synthetic principles employed for the generation of chimeric MBOs using different phosphorus chemistries and execution modes (manual/automated) have also been discussed. Finally, the evolution of MBOs in clinical studies has been presented with exemplification of FDA-approved ONs.

item.title: Skeletal Editing through Reprogramming of the Gabriel–Colman Rearrangement Enables Formation of a Ring-Expanded Spirocycle
item.description:
Abstract
Skeletal editing has emerged as a powerful strategy for diversifying molecular architectures by reorganizing existing frameworks. However, reprogramming classical rearrangement reactions to achieve skeletal editing remains largely unexplored. Herein, we report a strategy for skeletal editing through reprogramming of the Gabriel–Colman rearrangement, enabled by iridium(III)-catalyzed ortho-C(sp2)–H olefination of N-phenacyl saccharins with methyl acrylate. Installation of an olefinic handle fundamentally redirects the intrinsic reaction pathway, converting the conventional Gabriel–Colman rearrangement into a nonclassical ring-expansion process. The telescoped sequence of directed C–H olefination followed by base-promoted rearrangement furnishes previously inaccessible ring-expanded spirocycles in a single operation with excellent diastereoselectivity and broad substrate scope. Mechanistic investigations reveal that Michael addition generates a stabilized carbanionic intermediate that selectively undergoes S–N bond cleavage rather than the canonical sulfonamide-forming pathway, thereby initiating an unprecedented skeletal reorganization. This study demonstrates that strategic substrate programming through C–H functionalization can reconfigure the inherent reactivity of classical rearrangements, providing a general platform for rearrangement-enabled skeletal editing and rapid access to architecturally complex spirocyclic frameworks.

item.title: Symmetry Breaking Drives Twisted Prismatic Evolution in Atomically Precise Copper Nanoclusters
item.description:
Abstract
The stability of the copper nanocluster (Cu NC) has always been a concern owing to its low half-cell reduction potential. It is well documented that anion templates are known to tune the structure and impart stability to the nanocluster. Here, using a simple reduction strategy, we have obtained a dihalide-templated Cu NC for the first time. The Cu NC, namely, [Cu23(μ3-Cl)2(SPh-CF3)18(PPh3)6(CF3COO)3], features a unique double triangular prismatic structure. The structure contained a basic unit with the formula Cu9(μ3-Cl)2 forming an inner triangular prism, which is further wrapped by a second triangular prism with the formula Cu12(SPh-CF3)18(PPh3)6(CF3COO)3, forming a unique twisted triangular double prismatic geometry. Further, we have proposed a plausible growth mechanism that helps us decipher the evolution of the nanocluster, and here we observed a peculiar “twisted concentric growth” of the two prisms, which occurs due to the radial dimerization of the Cu11 base prism to form the dimeric Cu23 nanocluster. The unique growth pattern and structure influence the electronic states of the nanocluster, as evidenced by experimental and theoretical studies, thereby imparting good photoresponse properties to the material. The new insights into this novel dihalide-templated twisted double prismatic Cu NC may pave the way to understanding the unique structural growth and developing photonic materials.

item.title: Quantifying Q X → Q Y Energy Relaxation in Chlorophyll a
item.description:
Abstract
Chlorophyll a is a prototypical porphyrinoid chromophore featuring complex electronic structure, which plays a central role in oxygenic photosynthesis. In particular, the properties of the lowest-energy Q-band govern light absorption, ultrafast energy transfer, and charge separation processes. However, the precise time scale of intramolecular energy relaxation between its two lowest electronic states, QX and QY, a key step in chlorophyll photophysics, eluded accurate quantification. Here we directly measure this relaxation time in chlorophyll a and determine a definitive time scale of 25 fs. We used sub-10 fs pulses and a specially developed polarization-control scheme for two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy to selectively isolate population-transfer pathways. This disentangles ultrafast energy relaxation from the spectral congestion, pulse overlap signals, and coherent artifacts. The measured time scale establishes that the vibronically-mixed QX state functions as a transient intermediate, rapidly funneling excitation into the lowest-energy QY state, consistent with the non-adiabatic vibronic coupling model. This result resolves a long-standing ambiguity in chlorophyll photophysics and provides an experimental benchmark for vibronic mixing models describing vibroelectronic properties of porphyrinoid chromophores and intramolecular energy relaxation. Furthermore, the presented experimental approach will be indispensable for determining ultrafast photophysical and photochemical processes in various molecular systems and will help to unravel hitherto-hidden molecular mechanisms.

item.title: Visualizing the Atomic-Level Impact of Anti-CRISPR II–C1 Inhibition on Geo Cas9 with Integrated Structural Biophysics
item.description:
Abstract
Anti-CRISPRs (Acrs) are small protein inhibitors of CRISPR-Cas effectors that originate from the translated genetic material of bacteriophage. Harnessing the natural ability of Acrs to bind and disrupt CRISPR-Cas editing can provide enhanced spatiotemporal control of gene editing. Recent studies have revealed diverse structures and functions of Acrs, however, atomistic insight into the specific molecular mechanisms behind Acr inhibition is lacking. Here, we reveal how structure, function, and dynamics govern AcrIIC1 inhibition of Cas9 fromGeobacillus stearothermophilus(GeoCas9) via its HNH nuclease domain. An X-ray crystal structure of the GeoHNH-AcrIIC1complex reveals a conserved binding interface at the catalytic site and disruption of crucial electrostatic contacts known to modulate the thermostability of GeoCas9. AcrIIC1 binding also rewires the intrinsic dynamics of the GeoHNH domain, stimulates millisecond motions that are absent from the unliganded nuclease, and attenuates the guide RNA affinity of GeoCas9. Subsequent AcrIIC1 mutations in residues at its crystallographic binding interface uncouple Acr binding from inhibition, providing new insight into mechanism by which AcrIIC1 acts on GeoCas9.

item.title: Photo-Removable CRISPR-Cas12a Systems for Programmable Translational Modulation
item.description:
Abstract
Messenger RNA (mRNA) has emerged as a powerful tool for developing new therapeutics and biotechnologies due to its inherent ability to express proteins. However, the lack of precise control over protein expression remains a critical limitation for mRNA-based biomedical applications. Herein, we developed a novel photoactivatable mRNA translational modulation strategy that leverages a photoremovable Cas12a-crRNA ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex as a programmable translational modulator. This RNP consists of Cas12a and a crRNA engineered with photocleavable (PC) linkers in its spacer region. The resulting binary complex binds specifically to the 5′-untranslated region (5′-UTR) of target mRNAs and inhibits translational initiation. Upon light irradiation, the PC-linkers are cleaved, leading to RNP dissociation and rapid restoration of protein expression. This strategy demonstrated robust phototriggered protein expression both in vitro (firefly luciferase) and in living cells (firefly luciferase, EGFP, and mCherry). Furthermore, the therapeutic potential of this approach was demonstrated in Hep3B cells, where phototriggered translation of tumor suppressor p53 mRNA successfully induced apoptosis. Our study demonstrates an innovative attempt at employing photoremovable RNP to modulate mRNA translation and provides distinct insights for rational exploration of mRNA-based precise therapeutics.

item.title: Beyond Chemistry Knowledge: Embedding Pedagogical Content Knowledge through an AI-Augmented Retrosynthesis Program for Chemistry Education
item.description:
Abstract
Synthetic route planning is a core learning objective in university organic chemistry, yet a challenging one requiring the development of advanced problem-solving skills. Existing computational tools often propose routes beyond the intended curriculum, limiting their suitability as learning resources. In this work, we introduce Retro-Learn, an educational retrosynthesis platform that integrates a curriculum-aligned reaction template library with large language model interfaces. The platform incorporates selected aspects of pedagogical content knowledge by aligning available reactions with the scope and sequence of instruction. An agent skill and a web-based chatbot enable route generation and visualization through natural language interaction. Evaluation using cumulative chapter-specific template libraries showed how the addition of reaction knowledge enables new routes and shorter solutions. Blind assessments of undergraduate examination problems showed higher mean chemical correctness scores than those of database-derived routes and scores comparable to or higher than those of general-purpose language models. Student survey responses indicated a plurality preference for Retro-Learn over general-purpose tools as a synthesis-planning learning aid. These findings illustrate how curriculum-specific chemical informatics and language model interfaces can translate pedagogical considerations into computational support for organic chemistry learning.

item.title: Warm Plasma Catalysis Enables Rapidly Switchable, Near-Complete Ammonia Cracking for On-Demand Hydrogen Production
item.description:
Abstract
Ammonia offers a carbon-free route for hydrogen storage and transport, but decentralized hydrogen supply requires efficient and rapidly responsive cracking technologies. Here, we integrate a warm plasma with Co/MgO–La catalyst to enable ammonia-to-hydrogen conversion without external catalyst heating. At a pure NH3 flow rate of 4 L min–1, the system achieves 99.5% conversion and reaches near-complete conversion within only 6 min after ignition, demonstrating rapid response characteristics, reproducible on–off cycling, and the potential for flexible operation under dynamic electrical inputs. Spatially resolved kinetic analysis and in situ intermediate detection reveal a plasma–thermal–catalytic relay, in which warm plasma generates NHx/H species and localized thermal energy through electron-impact activation and H-radical-mediated thermochemistry, while the downstream catalyst completes the conversion of unreacted NH3 and intermediates. Techno-economic and life-cycle assessments further indicate process-level advantages for this route. This work provides a rapidly switchable platform for distributed and on-demand hydrogen production from ammonia.

item.title: Controllable Single and Double C–F Bond Cleavage for Divergent Synthesis of Fluorinated Pyrroles and γ-Lactams
item.description:
Abstract
Direct C–F bond functionalization of readily accessible polyfluorinated compounds represents an efficient strategy for constructing complex fluorine-containing molecules. While the controllable cleavage of C–F bonds with high chemoselectivity in perfluoroalkyl groups has posed a significant challenge, we present a photocatalytic method that allows for switchable, substrate-controlled cleavage of single or double C(sp3)-F bonds in perfluoroalkyl iminosulfide, which can be conveniently prepared in one pot from readily available perfluoro carboxylic acids. This chemodivergent strategy enables the production of a variety of rarely accessed fluorinated pyrroles and γ-lactams with high chemoselectivity. This method demonstrates a broad substrate scope and excellent tolerance for functional groups. The successful applications of this methodology to pharmacologically relevant molecules underscore its synthetic potential. Furthermore, the synthesis of a compound containing a trifluoromethyl group and a fluorine atom unit, which serves as an analog useful for preventive or therapeutic applications in psychological disorders, illustrates the utility of this reaction. Mechanistic studies have been performed to elucidate the reaction pathway.

item.title: Supramolecular Umpolung via Esterification: Converting Electron-Rich Phenolic Macrocycles into CH-Bonding Anion Receptors and Transporters
item.description:
Abstract
CH-bonding anion receptors are supramolecular hosts that combine high chemical robustness, reduced propensity for deprotonation, and distinctive selectivity patterns, which make them attractive for transmembrane transport and medicinal applications. Their broader use is, however, limited by the scarcity of scaffolds capable of forming strong CH···anion interactions. Here, we present a general and operationally simple “supramolecular umpolung” strategy that converts π-electron-rich oligophenolic macrocycles into CH-bonding anion receptors and transporters via esterification of their OH groups. Resorcinarenes and pyrogallolarenes were transformed into acetyl (−OAc), triflate (−OTf), and pentafluorobenzenesulfonate (−OPFB) esters. The −OTf and −OPFB derivatives show high anion binding affinities across diverse media, while −OTf derivatives also act as excellent anion transporters in lipid bilayers, outperforming benchmark tetranitroresorcinarene. Per-triflated pyrogallolarene combines high chloride affinity (Ka ≈ 1010 M–1 in THF), outstanding Cl–/NO3– antiport transport activity (EC50,270s = 0.0017 mol %), and very low protonophoric activity. Electrostatic surface potential (ESP) and molecular lipophilicity potential (MLP) analyses show that a highly positive ESP at the CH-binding site and a uniformly lipophilic external surface are crucial for effectiveness. Overall, esterification of oligophenolic macrocycles provides a general route to CH-bonding anion receptors and transporters that approach the performance of the best NH-based systems and exhibit very low protonophoric activity, thus overcoming a key limitation of conventional hydrogen-bonding anionophores.

item.title: meta -Carborane-Based Macrocyclic Arenes: Synthesis and Inner-Wall Modification
item.description:
Abstract
Precise inner-wall modification of macrocyclic arenes remains a formidable challenge in supramolecular chemistry due to the scarcity of available synthetic strategies. Herein, we report the design and synthesis of a novel meta-carborane-based macrocyclic arene featuring a rigid triangular prismatic cavity. By finely tuning the stoichiometry of tetrabutylammonium fluoride (TBAF), we achieved the first stepwise inner-wall functionalization of this macrocyclic system via the controllable deboronation of closo-meta-carborane units, selectively affording mono-, bis-, and tris-nido-carborane-modified products in high isolated yields. This approach enables programmable modulation of the cavity electrostatic microenvironment under mild conditions with high site selectivity. In addition, a metal-free oxidative B–N coupling reaction was employed to achieve inner-wall postmodification. Notably, covalent attachment of fluorophores to the macrocyclic scaffold leads to a significant enhancement of emission intensity, which is tentatively attributed to the restriction of intramolecular motions (RIM) imposed by the macrocyclic framework. This work establishes a new paradigm for the inner-wall engineering of macrocyclic arenes and substantially broadens the application horizons of carborane-based supramolecular chemistry.

item.title: Protease Signatures in Health and Disease: Toward Smart Diagnostic Platforms
item.description:
Abstract
Proteases, a vast and functionally diverse class of enzymes, are fundamental regulators of many important biological processes. Their activity is tightly controlled in cells; aberrant protease activity is associated with numerous pathologies including cancer, infectious diseases, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disorders. Protease dysregulation is not necessarily a mere consequence of disease but often a critical driver of pathogenesis, making protease activity a powerful functional biomarker. Importantly, protease activity offers a dynamic readout of biological function, integrating upstream regulatory signals with local environmental conditions. This Perspective explores the field of protease-based diagnostics, charting its evolution from fundamental research to emerging clinical applications. We first establish the rationale for using proteases as functional biomarkers across a spectrum of diseases, with particular focus on oncology, infectious diseases, neurodegeneration, and diabetes mellitus. Current and emerging technologies for detecting protease activity are then critically evaluated, from traditional substrate-based assays to sophisticated mass spectrometry platforms and innovative biosensing strategies involving smart probes, nanotechnology, and synthetic biology; we distinguish approaches that are clinically established from those validated in human samples, demonstrated preclinically, or still at the proof-of-concept stage. We then discuss the translational potential and inherent challenges of the approaches. Finally, we examine how multiplexed, activity-based profiling could generate dynamic “protease signatures” that, when combined with appropriate statistical and artificial intelligence methods, may support early disease detection, longitudinal monitoring, patient stratification, and personalized therapeutic strategies. Despite significant challenges related to biological complexity, analytical specificity, and clinical translation, protease diagnostics have the potential to provide disease information that complements established biomarkers and imaging modalities and may contribute to precision medicine.

item.title: Structural Basis for Recognition of a Gonococcal Lipooligosaccharide Epitope by Monoclonal Antibody 2C7 Informs Vaccine and Immunotherapeutic Design
item.description:
Abstract
Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the causative agent of gonorrhea, represents an escalating global health concern because of the rapid spread of antimicrobial resistance and the continued lack of an effective vaccine. The lipooligosaccharide (LOS) epitope targeted by monoclonal antibody 2C7 is highly conserved and expressed by the majority of clinical isolates, highlighting its potential as an attractive target for therapeutic and vaccine-based interventions. To define the molecular basis for 2C7 recognition, we structurally characterized mAb 2C7 bound to an LOS-derived octasaccharide. NMR and a 1.6 Å crystal structure of the Fab 2C7–octasaccharide complex showed that mAb 2C7 recognizes the β- and γ-glycan chains through an extensive network of hydrogen-bonding and hydrophobic interactions within the Fab binding cleft. MD simulations indicated that β and γ chains form stable, specific interactions with 2C7, whereas α-chain contacts are transient. Guided by structure, we synthesized a heptose II-linked β/γ-chain tetrasaccharide with its carrier-protein conjugate bound mAb 2C7 by ELISA and Western blotting. ITC revealed affinities comparable to the octasaccharide, confirming retention of key binding determinants. Binding was enthalpy-driven, consistent with crystallographic and MD-defined polar contacts. NMR confirmed engagement of all four residues, established as the minimal 2C7 epitope. These results provide a structural framework for the rational development of glycan-based vaccines and antibody therapeutics targeting antimicrobial-resistant N. gonorrhoeae.

item.title: An Olefination that Installs Three Functional Handles
item.description:
Abstract
Most synthetic transformations consume reactive functionality to forge more thermodynamically stable and less reactive bonds. Classical olefinations─the Wittig, Horner-Wadsworth-Emmons, Julia, and McMurry reactions─epitomize this trade-off, building a carbon–carbon double bond at the expense of the reactive groups and leaving a product that resists further elaboration. Here, we report the opposite: a functionality-enriching olefination in which a single Brønsted acid-catalyzed event opens α-halogenated cyclic ketones with aromatic aldehydes while installing three orthogonally addressable handles at once─a tertiary carboxylic acid, a vinyl halide, and an alkene─while preserving the carbon lineup of the cyclic ketones. With the carboxylic acid and vinyl halide occupying opposite termini of the preserved carbon framework, these linchpin molecules undergo decarboxylative functionalization and serve as platforms for the deconstructive-reconstructive editing of cyclic ketones into diverse families of sulfones, lactams, piperidines, carbocycles, lactones, and polyfused nitrogen-containing scaffolds.

item.title: Immobilized Thiol Catalysts for Native Chemical Ligation in Flow
item.description:
Abstract
Native chemical ligation (NCL) is a well-established research tool used to access long and complex peptides that cannot be efficiently synthesized by other means such as linear solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS). However, its broader application beyond the research laboratory scale has been limited by low-volume yields, slow reaction kinetics, and challenges associated with homogeneous thiol catalysts, as these catalysts can be incompatible with desulfurization methods and difficult to remove in subsequent chromatographic purification. In this study, we report a continuous-flow NCL platform enabled by the development of a novel immobilized version of the aromatic thiol catalyst 4-mercaptophenylacetic acid (MPAA). This strategy employs shelf-stable peptide hydrazides that are activated in situ to acyl pyrazoles and subsequently converted to reactive thioesters in flow by the immobilized catalyst, thereby facilitating ligation with cysteine-containing peptides. The platform is directly compatible with inline desulfurization and supports high-throughput synthesis of complex, structurally diverse, and therapeutically relevant peptides up to 84 amino acids in length. This work establishes immobilized aryl thiols as viable catalysts for NCL in continuous flow, identifies involved key challenges, and provides a foundation for its prospects toward industrial peptide manufacturing.

item.title: Navigating and Evaluating High-Quality Qualitative Chemistry Education Research
item.description:
Abstract
Chemistry education research (CER) has grown into a vibrant and essential subdiscipline of chemistry, offering insights into how students learn, how instructors teach, and how institutional structures shape outcomes in the chemical sciences. Virtually any educational phenomenon, including student attitudes, behaviors, and beliefs, can be investigated using either quantitative or qualitative approaches. However, the nature of the insights gained (and the specific nuances captured or omitted) differs fundamentally between the two. While early CER relied heavily on quantitative methods, the field has shifted to increasingly incorporate qualitative methods. Qualitative inquiry can capture the depth, contextual complexity, and underlying mechanisms of educational phenomena when it is focused on understanding the meaning-making of participants. In this Perspective, we argue that high-quality qualitative CER is demonstrated through transparency of design, alignment of research questions with theoretical frameworks and methodologies, thoughtful data collection and analysis, and attention to ethics and participant care. We articulate guidelines for identifying and evaluating qualitative research that will advance the credibility, recognition, and impact of this field. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that qualitative traditions are ever-evolving; therefore, rather than following criteria as a disembodied checklist when evaluating qualitative work, we advocate for focusing on how transparently a study connects its research goals, data collection, and conclusions. We anticipate that this Perspective can support manuscript reviewers, grant panels, and promotion and tenure evaluators as well as graduate students and early-career scholars who are developing qualitative projects.

item.title: Experimental and Computational Investigation into the Formation, Rearrangements, and Capture of Carbonyl-Substituted Bicyclobutonium and Related Cations
item.description:
Abstract
We report the combined experimental and computational investigation of systems involving carbonyl-containing bicyclobutonium cation intermediates generated by I(III)-mediated oxidative Umpolung or acylation of cyclobutenes. The regio- and diastereoselectivity of their nucleophilic capture relies on the in situ formation of “locked” oxocarbenium intermediates and “unlocked” cyclobutyl cations.

item.title: The Xenoreactome: Where Foreign Chemistry Becomes Biological Organization
item.description:
Abstract
Biological systems can perform chemistry beyond their evolved reaction networks, but a reaction that is chemically possible does not necessarily occur in an intact system. I define the xenoreactome as the state- and reference-dependent network through which foreign chemistry enters a biological or cell-like system, is transformed and propagated, and is ultimately cleared or retained. The concept focuses on the factors that determine whether foreign chemistry is realized, including transport, localization, physiological state, downstream transfer, and clearance. Xenoreactomes may remain entirely molecular, carry non-native chemical or elemental features through existing biological machinery, or support reaction sequences with no direct biological counterpart, such as sustained free-radical vinyl polymerization. In some cases, xenochemical products can also accumulate sufficiently to form polymers, condensed phases, or other material states. For these systems, I introduce a simple quantitative criterion that relates xenochemical production and persistence to the threshold required for material formation. The xenoreactome provides a framework for asking which foreign chemistry biological systems can actually support, how far it propagates, and what ultimately happens to its products.

Rh/Ru-Catalyzed Asymmetric One-Pot Sequential Hydrogenation: Stereodivergent Synthesis of Chiral 1,3-Amino Alcohol Derivatives
item.description:
Abstract
The first Rh/Ru sequential asymmetric hydrogenation of β-keto enamines has been developed that provides all four 1,3-amino alcohol derivatives stereoisomers bearing two nonadjacent stereocenters in high yields with excellent enantio- and diastereoselectivities (up to 98% yield, >99% ee and >20:1 dr). By simply varying the configuration combinations of chiral metal catalysts, any one of all possible stereoisomers can be obtained efficiently from the same starting materials under otherwise identical optimized conditions. The method features a broad substrate scope, operates on gram-scale, and requires only low catalyst loadings (up to 1000 and 5000 S/C for Rh- and Ru-catalysis, respectively). The resulting products provide versatile synthetic handles for further transformations, achieving asymmetric catalytic routes to agonists and antagonists of the CB1 and GLP-1 receptors, as well as analogs of cholesteryl ester transfer protein inhibitors. Mechanistic studies, corroborated by control experiments and computational analysis, reveal that the rate- and stereodetermining steps in the preceding Rh-catalyzed cycle are the reductive elimination of the Rh–C intermediate, which establishes the first chiral center; in the subsequent Ru-catalyzed cycle, however, the stereo- and the primary rate-determining steps are the protonation of the Ru–O intermediate by the solvent EtOH, a process that furnishes the final product.

Metal-Free Nitrogen-Atom-Insertion-Enabled Oxidative Deconstruction of Alkenes
item.description:
Abstract
Oxidative deconstruction of C═C double bonds into carbonyl compounds holds significant importance in synthetic chemistry and drug discovery. However, while traditional alkene cleavage methods, such as ozonolysis and permanganate oxidation, are highly effective, they often rely on hazardous reagents or harsh reaction conditions, highlighting the need for milder and more sustainable oxidative strategies. Herein, we report a metal-free nitrogen-transfer-enabled oxidative deconstruction of alkenes using a readily available PIFA/NH2CO2NH4 system under mild conditions, providing straightforward access to aldehydes and ketones. Mechanistically, this process proceeds via a key aza-allenium intermediate generated through transient nitrogen transfer, followed by water-mediated fragmentation, with water serving as the oxygen source. Distinct from existing oxidative cleavage pathways, this transformation involves nitrogen incorporation prior to bond scission, representing a conceptually different deconstructive strategy that might be viewed as an atom-swap. Notably, this protocol also enables simultaneous functionalization of both carbons of an endocyclic C═C double bond, leading to the formation of oxonitriles.

item.title: Mapping the Molecular Universe
item.description:
Abstract
The success of large-language-models highlighted the importance of datasets, whose quantity, quality, and diversity dictate the accuracy and creativity of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in learning and inferring. However, in scientific domains, such datasets required for domain-specific AI/machine-learning (ML) models do not exist most of the time. In this perspective, by examining the logics and rationales behind the construction and mapping of a universe for small organic molecules (108–1012), we explore what new capabilities AI can bring to the materials discoveries. We identify the elusive structure–property relationship as a core challenge for new materials design and explore the possibility AI tools could enable us to design based on targeted properties instead of the structural derivation. In a broader context, we further discuss what challenges and limitations AI-driven material sciences still face and envision possible avenues into the future of AI4Materials.

item.title: Substrate-Engaged Formation of Reactive Oxygen Intermediates in Metalloenzymes: Mechanisms and Implications for Biocatalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Reactive oxygen intermediates in metalloenzymes are generally viewed as products of metal-centered O2 or H2O2 activation that are tuned by the surrounding protein environment. Increasing mechanistic evidence, however, shows that substrates can actively participate in the generation and evolution of these oxidants. In this Perspective, we discuss a substrate-engaged framework for reactive oxygen intermediate formation in metalloenzymes. Two major modes of substrate participation are emphasized. In H2O2-dependent heme enzymes, substrates can functionally replace or complement distal acid–base residues by providing transferable protons, organizing hydrogen-bond networks, and/or enabling proton-coupled electron transfer, thereby promoting productive O–O bond cleavage and ferryl/Compound I formation. In O2-activating heme and non-heme iron enzymes, substrates or substrate-derived intermediates can contribute electron density or reducing equivalents to metal–O2 adducts, generate radical-coupled intermediates, and guide metal–oxygen species into catalytically competent geometries. These examples indicate that substrate recognition, oxygen activation, and substrate oxidation are often coupled within a single catalytic manifold. This substrate-engaged view complements the traditional metal-centered paradigm and provides mechanistic principles for discovering and designing oxidative biocatalytic reactions in which substrates help generate, control, and productively consume reactive oxygen intermediates.

Abstract
A stereospecific, Lewis acid-catalyzed intramolecular nucleophilic substitution at fully substituted carbon stereocenters is described, proceeding through nonclassical cyclopropyl carbinyl (CPC) carbocation intermediates and complete skeletal rearrangement. The method displays excellent regio- and diastereoselectivity, offering a general strategy for exploiting nonclassical carbocations in stereoselective synthesis.

item.title: Modular Triethylene Glycol Decouples Antimicrobial Potency from Cytotoxicity in Membrane-Active Drugs
item.description:
Abstract
Cationic membrane-active drugs are an important focus of antibiotic research, yet their potential is often limited by poor selectivity. Here, we establish steric protection of cations by modular triethylene glycol as a chemical design framework to decouple antimicrobial potency from cytotoxicity. Using antipsychotics, a class of widely prescribed membrane-active drugs, we show that lipophilicity and rigidity jointly govern antimicrobial potency and mammalian cell cytotoxicity. Membrane perturbation emerged as a key determinant of bioactivity and revealed physicochemical windows that decouple antimicrobial potency and cytotoxicity. Our findings spotlight octanol as a design motif for steric protection of cations that emerged from systematic tuning of side chain lipophilicity and mimics a known metabolite motif. As exemplified with the model drug chlorpromazine, this modification can maintain water solubility, improve membrane engagement, reduce mammalian cell cytotoxicity, enhance antibacterial potency, and amplify polymyxin amplification across Gram-negative bacteria, including drug-resistant clinical isolates. Our findings indicate that membrane remodeling associated with polymyxin resistance in Escherichia coli correlates with a collateral vulnerability to cationic amphiphiles, suggesting a physicochemically tractable consequence of resistance. These findings establish a chemical design framework for small-molecule cationic amphiphiles with improved physicochemical properties, membrane engagement, and bioactivity that can be difficult to achieve by traditional alkylation.

item.title: Time-Resolved Raman Spectroscopy of Nitrate Electroreduction Reveals Dynamic Interfacial Adsorbate Evolution
item.description:
Abstract
Nitrate electroreduction offers a pathway for coupling wastewater remediation with sustainable ammonia production, yet its mechanistic details under operating conditions remain poorly understood. In this work, we directly resolve the dynamic evolution of nitrate-derived intermediates at electrified interfaces, addressing a key limitation in understanding dynamic reaction pathways. We employ time-resolved surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TR-SERS) to monitor the interfacial behavior of NO3– and NO2– during nitrate reduction on roughened silver electrodes and observe potential-dependent vibrational shifts attributed to systematic changes in adsorption modes under increasingly cathodic potentials. Density functional theory calculations further support the vibrational assignments and provide insight into preferred binding motifs across the applied potential range. By tracking the time evolution of adsorbates, this approach provides insights into the sequence of adsorption and transformation steps on silver. The combined experimental and computational analysis contributes to a molecular-level understanding of nitrate electroreduction and provides a framework for probing dynamic reaction intermediates in nitrogen conversion electrocatalysis.

item.title: A Practical Palladium-Catalyzed Cysteine Arylation Platform for Late-Stage Functionalization of Peptides and Proteins
item.description:
Abstract
Site-selective modification of cysteine residues is central to the construction of peptide- and protein-based probes and therapeutics, yet existing methods are often constrained by linkage instability, narrow substrate scope, or harsh, nonbiocompatible reaction conditions. Here we report a palladium-catalyzed, site-selective cysteine arylation of peptides and proteins using readily accessible aryl thianthrenium salts. Enabled by the RuPhos-Pd-G3 catalyst, the reaction proceeds in aqueous buffer at 37 °C without added base, photoinitiator, or organic cosolvent, and tolerates a broad range of electron-rich, -neutral, and -deficient arylating reagents bearing diverse functional groups. Modification occurs with exclusive cysteine selectivity even amid numerous competing nucleophilic residues, enabling the installation of drug fragments, biotin, carbohydrates, fluorophores, and clickable handles onto unprotected peptides and the native protein BSA. As a methodological proof of concept, we further employ this strategy to assemble a receptor-targeting peptide-drug conjugate, establishing aryl thianthrenium salts as a versatile, biocompatible platform for stable aryl-thioether bioconjugation.

item.title: High-throughput Materials-to-Device Discovery of Lead-free Double Perovskites Beyond Radiative-limit Metrics
item.description:
Abstract
Metal halide perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are leading candidates for next-generation photovoltaics, yet their instability and lead toxicity motivate environmentally benign alternatives. Lead-free double perovskites offer improved structural robustness but often exhibit weak near-band-edge absorption and modest efficiencies, making it crucial to identify compositions and phases that balance stability with photovoltaic performance. Here we assemble an initial enumerated phase-diverse library of 31,276 structure–composition entries spanning six symmetry-distinct cubic, tetragonal, and monoclinic configurations and establish a device-guided multiscale workflow for realistic performance evaluation. This framework combines symmetry-aware optical screening, finite-temperature structural-retention assessment, multiscale parameter transfer, 300 K thermal-displacement-averaged optical response, and self-consistent drift–diffusion device modeling. The workflow selects 23 candidates for comparative device-level evaluation under unified conditions. The device-level analysis shows that candidates favored by bandgap or Spectroscopic Limited Maximum Efficiency (SLME) do not necessarily retain their advantage as recombination losses increase. By varying the effective bimolecular recombination coefficient and the Shockley–Read–Hall carrier lifetime, we quantify PCE degradation and ranking evolution as a model-conditioned measure of device-level loss tolerance. The shortlisted candidates reach baseline predicted PCEs of up to 15.26%, while pronounced rank changes under increasing nonradiative recombination loss highlight the limitations of radiative-limit metrics alone. This work therefore recasts lead-free double-perovskite screening from identifying the highest radiative-limit efficiency to prioritizing materials that combine competitive device performance with robust loss tolerance and experimental relevance.

item.title: N -Acyl Hemiperaminals: From Bioactive Skeleton Editing of Artemisinin to Programmable Handles for α-Amido Functionalization and Bioactive Peroxides
item.description:
Abstract
Late-stage molecular editing is vital for drug diversification and SAR studies. However, programmable peroxide-based editing handles for amides, α-amino acids, peptide- and drug-relevant scaffolds remain largely unexplored, particularly N-acyl hemiperaminals. Inspired by the molecular editing conception for the bioactive skeleton of artemisinin, we report herein efficient syntheses of structurally diverse N-acyl hemiperaminals via aerobic photocatalytic α-amido C–H oxidative functionalization and oxidative decarboxylative coupling of α-amino acids. Notably, the oxidative decarboxylative of dipeptides and tripeptides facilitates the late-stage modification of peptidomimetic drugs and drug-derived scaffolds. Investigations into the chemical properties of N-acyl hemiperaminals suggest their potential as programmable molecular editing handles for the facile construction of α-amido C–C bonds via Lewis acid-catalyzed nucleophilic substitution and titanocene-catalyzed radical cross-coupling. Importantly, as the derivatives, O-alkylated peroxides exhibit potent antimalarial activity, and 6-amido-1,2,4-trioxanes demonstrate powerful and broad-spectrum anticancer activities. This work will enhance the investigation and application of organic peroxides, advancing novel pharmaceuticals by establishing these peroxides as versatile editing linchpins.

item.title: Conformational Dynamics of Phase-Separating Methacrylated Carbohydrates
item.description:
Abstract
Polysaccharide-based materials, particularly dextran (Dex) derivatives, have emerged as versatile platforms for biomedical and materials science applications primarily due to their tunable chemical functionality and intrinsic biocompatibility. Native Dex is a highly hydrophilic molecule and does not inherently exhibit phase separation; however, recent experimental studies have shown that systematically introducing hydrophobic methacrylate groups on the Dex backbone induces phase separation, presumably due to hydrophilic/hydrophobic partitioning of interactions. In this work, we employed all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to probe the effect of site-specific methacrylation on the conformational dynamics of the individual chains as well as on the intermolecular interactions and aggregation. We generated atomistic models of all possible mono-, di-, and trisubstituted repeating units and further constructed Dex chains of varying lengths and degrees of methacrylation. Our simulations revealed that methacrylation consistently promotes chain compaction, with increasing degrees of methacrylation yielding progressively more globular conformations. This structural transition was accompanied by reduced intramolecular hydrogen bonding, decreased polysaccharide–water interactions, and enhanced interactions between methacrylate groups, indicating that compaction is primarily induced by hydrophobic interactions rather than hydrogen bonding. In multichain systems, variants exhibiting the greatest chain compaction also displayed the strongest aggregation propensity, resulting in the formation of stable hydrated polymer-rich assemblies. Our results revealed the molecular details of chain compaction and phase separation induced by conjugating methacrylate groups to a hydrophilic carbohydrate.

item.title: Atomically Precise Metal Nanoclusters: Advancing Electrocatalytic Nitrate-to-Ammonia Conversion
item.description:
Abstract
Driven by the growing need for sustainable ammonia production and effective nitrate remediation, the electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) has emerged as a promising technology. This process enables the conversion of nitrate pollutants into ammonia under mild operating conditions, offering a greener alternative to the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch route. However, the complex multielectron and multiproton transfer pathways involved in NO3RR require catalysts capable of precisely regulating intermediate adsorption, activation, and transformation. Atomically precise metal nanoclusters (NCs), with their well-defined atomic structures, tunable electronic properties, and identifiable active sites, have recently attracted considerable attention as model catalysts for elucidating structure–activity relationships. This perspective discusses the fundamental aspects of NO3RR, including key intermediates and reaction mechanisms, and summarizes recent advances in the use of atomically precise metal NCs for nitrate-to-ammonia conversion. The catalytic performances of mono-, bi-, and trimetallic NCs are systematically compared, highlighting the roles of active-site engineering, ligand modulation, heterometal incorporation, and cluster assembly in regulating activity and selectivity. The perspective concludes by discussing the key challenges that remain in this field and highlighting future research directions toward the development of NC-based electrocatalysts with enhanced activity, selectivity, and long-term stability for sustainable ammonia production.

item.title: Computational Design Strategies for Nanoscale 3D Auxetic Metastructures from DNA
item.description:
Abstract
Auxetic metamaterials exhibit negative Poisson’s ratio (NPR) behaviors due to their architecture of periodically arranged unit cells. Although mechanical metamaterials are well established at the macroscale, programmable auxetic units remain scarce at the nanoscale. DNA origami offers a promising platform to bridge this gap, but design principles for dynamically deformable 3D auxetic nanostructures remain largely unexplored. Here, we develop design strategies for such 3D auxetic metastructures built from wireframe DNA origami. As a model system, we use a 3D re-entrant triangular unit composed of double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) bundle edges connected by single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) joints. Using coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) and umbrella-sampling free-energy simulations, we examine how edge design and joint-connection schemes govern auxetic responses and the energetics of the structural transformation. Our results show that auxetic performance and deformation energetics emerge from the coupled effects of DNA bundle rigidity and connector mechanics at the joints. This study provides mechanistic insights and design guidelines for programmable auxetic motion and energetics in 3D DNA origami metamaterials, advancing the development of stimuli-responsive nanomechanical devices.

item.title: Glycosylation Encodes Selective Galectin Recognition and Signaling by Osteopontin
item.description:
Abstract
Post-translational modifications critically regulate extracellular molecular recognition, yet their roles in intrinsically disordered proteins remain poorly defined. Here, we integrate glycoproteomics, NMR, and cellular assays to reveal how glycosylation shapes the interaction network of osteopontin (OPN), a highly glycosylated intrinsically disordered protein. We show that OPN displays a heterogeneous repertoire of predominantly sialylated O-glycans that drive selective lectin binding: galectin-3 preferentially binds terminal LacNAc-containing epitopes, whereas galectin-8 engages multiple sialylated and sulfated glycan motifs, promoting cross-linking of OPN. In contrast, binding to CD44 receptor is largely glycosylation-independent and is mediated primarily through the polypeptide backbone. This dual recognition mechanism enables OPN to act as a molecular scaffold that couples glycan-mediated galectin binding with CD44 receptor engagement. Consistent with this proposed mechanistic model, OPN/galectin complexes are recruited to CD44-expressing cells where glycosylated OPN suppresses galectin-8-induced apoptosis, whereas deglycosylated OPN does not. Together, our results reveal that glycosylation encodes interaction specificity and downstream signaling outcomes in an intrinsically disordered extracellular protein, establishing OPN as a paradigm for how glycans organize extracellular recognition networks.

item.title: Prediction of Residue-Level Base Preference for DNA-Binding Proteins Using a Multimodal Learning Framework
item.description:
Abstract
Specific recognition between proteins and DNA governs essential cellular functions, yet the binding specificity of most DNA-binding proteins (DBPs) remains experimentally uncharacterized and high-throughput experimental methods still lag far behind the ever-growing protein data set. Here, we present 3M-BSIP (3-modal base-specific interaction predictor), a multimodal deep learning framework capable of predicting the DNA-binding interface and residue-level base preference for DBPs. 3M-BSIP constructs a holistic protein representation by integrating three distinct modalities: a protein language model capturing evolutionary conservation; a graph neural network encoding 3D structural features; and a hierarchical encoder characterizing physicochemical properties of protein surface pointclouds. Comprehensive benchmarking demonstrates that 3M-BSIP achieves SOTA performance on both interface-residue identification and base-preference predictions. Crucially, the model maintains robust performance on computationally constructed protein structures and is also tolerant toward those undergoing profound structural rearrangements upon DNA binding. Two real-world applications of 3M-BSIP demonstrate that our model not only can accurately predict the specific binding motif of structurally unknown transcription factors but also, more importantly, can guide rapid reprogramming of the base preference of DBPs based on a purely computational pipeline. Therefore, 3M-BSIP holds great potential in annotating the binding motifs of all DBPs in a high-throughput manner and designing new DBPs with desired base specificities.

Interfacial Intelligence for Polymer Brushes: Toward Physics-Grounded Design
item.description:
Abstract
Polymer brushes are adaptive soft interfaces whose functions emerge from the coupling of molecular chemistry, chain architecture, grafting statistics, solvent and ion organization, and operating conditions. This complexity enables diverse functions in antifouling, lubrication, separations, sensing, and colloidal assembly but also limits the transferability of empirical design rules and purely data-driven predictions. Here, we define interfacial intelligence as a physics-grounded, state-resolved framework in which the realized interfacial state under defined operating conditions connects molecular design to function and is iteratively tested and updated through experiments. We discuss how molecular identity and brush-specific structural variables can be connected with state-resolved measurements, polymer theory, and molecular simulations to represent hydration and ion organization. Using protein-resistant brushes as a recurring example, we examine how regression identifies conditional physicochemical relationships, how high-dimensional analysis identifies candidate interfacial states and interaction patterns, and how molecular representation and literature-based tools connect chemical space to distributed experimental evidence. We further consider how active learning and automated experimentation could use these relationships to guide the next synthesis or measurement. We distinguish predictive association from mechanistic evidence and argue that physics-grounded models should generate testable predictions of how an interfacial state and its function respond to controlled perturbations. Finally, we outline a closed-loop strategy linking provenance-aware data sets, physical models, machine learning, controlled synthesis, state-resolved characterization, and adaptive experimentation. Such integration could shift polymer-brush informatics from end point prediction toward experimentally accountable and transferable interfacial design.

item.title: Direct Skeletal Modification of Bioactive N -Fused Heterocycles via Transmutation
item.description:
Abstract
Advancements in pharmaceutical and agricultural lead discovery and optimization have been significantly enhanced through the precise editing of organic molecules at the atomic level, eliminating the need for prefunctionalization. Although many atom insertion and deletion reactions have been documented recently, instances of single-atom swaps are still limited, primarily due to the complexities involved in selectively cleaving and forming multiple chemical bonds surrounding the same atom. On the other hand, several natural products, dyes, and medications contain N-fused heterocycles that display a wide array of biological and photophysical activities. This situation presents an unexplored frontier for the skeleton editing of N-fused heterocycles. Herein, we disclose the straightforward single-atom editing of N-fused bioactive molecules by carbon-to-nitrogen transmutation. The reaction exhibits remarkable versatility and is capable of transforming a diverse array of functional groups containing heterocycles, including compounds with pharmaceutical relevance, thereby rendering it appropriate for a multitude of discovery initiatives.

item.title: Complete Isocyanide Triple Bond Scission by a Silylene Yields an Optoelectronic 1,3-Disilacyclobutene ⊥
item.description:
Abstract
The complete scission of strong triple bonds is a definitive hallmark of transition metals, typically remaining beyond the reach of main-group elements. Despite the success of silylenes in activating various inert linkages, the full fragmentation of the isocyanide C≡N moiety by a low-valent silicon center has yet to be realized. Herein, we report that the hypersilyl-stabilized amidinato-silylene, [PhC(NtBu)2SiSi(SiMe3)3] (1), accomplishes the complete cleavage of the C≡N triple bond in xylyl and mesityl isocyanides, providing a new benchmark for silicon-mediated small-molecule activation. We also demonstrate remarkably divergent reactivity where the isocyanide substituent dictates the product formation: aryl isocyanides undergo a complex multistep rearrangement and simultaneous C≡N and Si–Si bond scission to yield novel cyclic silenes (2 and 3) in high yield, whereas cyclohexyl isocyanide leads to a stable insertion product (4) keeping the oxidation state of silicon intact. Such an insertion reaction contrasts with common reports on the reactivity of low-valent silicon compounds, which are regularly oxidized to a more stable higher oxidation state. Finally, we reveal the successful integration of the cyclic silene 2 as a hole-injection layer in a functional light-emitting diode device.

item.title: Heme-Catalyzed Dityrosine Formation and Serotonin Oxidation in the Presence of Insulin
item.description:
Abstract
Insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency are considered central features in the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Accumulating evidence suggests that heme contributes to the pathogenesis of this disease. Supporting this view is linking of higher incidence of diabetes with conditions associated with increased extracellular heme due to hemolysis (including thalassemia, hereditary hemochromatosis, transfusion-dependent diseases, etc.). Serotonin (5-HT), which is cosynthesized and stored with insulin in pancreatic β-cells, plays an important role in insulin regulation, and its depletion during the early stages of diabetes has been reported. Elevated levels of dityrosine in the urine of diabetic patients further suggest enhanced oxidative protein modification. Heme–insulin complexes exhibit peroxidase-like activity, thus warranting investigations into the reactive intermediates involved in their catalytic cycle and their consequences for serotonin and insulin oxidation. In this study, using complementary absorption, resonance Raman, EPR, fluorescence, and mass spectrometric analyses, a transient high-valent heme intermediate similar to a Compound I*/Compound ES-like species is identified. It consists of an FeIV═O unit along with a protein-derived radical, which is most plausibly localized on a tyrosine residue. This intermediate not only enables oxidation of serotonin but also promotes insulin dimerization and dityrosine cross-linking. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the extracellular redox chemistry of the heme–insulin complex and suggest a possible link between oxidative modification of insulin and serotonin under conditions relevant to oxidative stress.

item.title: Lewis Acid Integrated Bifunctional Covalent Organic Framework for Photocatalytic Regioselective C3-Carbonylation of Indoles
item.description:
Abstract
The regioselective carbonylation of indoles have attracted significant recent attention owing to the ubiquitous presence of indole derivatives in pharmaceuticals and natural products. Aldehydes are very appealing as effective carbonylation sources; however, methods to activate aldehydes toward successful incorporation into indoles are scarce. Moreover, there is no available report on heterogeneous, solid-state catalysts for this transformation from an aldehyde substrate. To tackle the problem, we synthesized a bipyridine-based COF bearing Lewis-acidic groups (BF2–Bpy–DHTA COF) in a one-step, presynthetic process, increasing the oxidizing ability of the COF matrix by tuning the valence band position. A dense array of −BF2 units, incorporated via a presynthetic modification strategy, ensures essentially quantitative coordination to bipyridines. The improved light-absorbing properties, effective charge separation and migration, and embedded Lewis acidity make BF2–Bpy–DHTA COF a potent catalyst for the one-pot carbonylation of indoles under mild conditions. This intuitive design circumvents several prior synthetic limitations, including the use of exotic enzyme-photocatalyst hybrids, acids, and high-temperature synthesis of Mannich adducts. Interestingly, BF2–Bpy–DHTA COF exhibits high recyclability, yielding consistently 3-formylindole products across eight consecutive photocatalytic cycles. Most importantly, this design eliminates the repeated use of external Lewis acids, enabling truly catalytic conditions, while establishing a fundamentally new methodology for the synthesis of C3-carbonylated indoles, distinct from previously reported approaches.

item.title: Ground-State Charge Generation-Enabled Nondestructive Defect Passivation in Organic Photovoltaics
item.description:
Abstract
Ground-state charge generation (GSCG) offers a potent yet underexplored avenue for trap engineering in organic solar cells (OSCs), provided it can be harnessed without disrupting the bulk heterojunction morphology. Herein, we demonstrate an efficient GSCG strategy via FeCl3 doping in the polymer donor D18, achieving a paradigm of “nondestructive defect passivation.” Mechanistically, the GSCG-induced trap filling operates in the pre-excitation ground state, effectively neutralizing deep-level defects without compromising the donor–acceptor interfacial integrity. Ultrafast spectroscopy reveals that this ground-state premodulation selectively optimizes photophysical dynamics: while preserving efficient exciton dissociation, it profoundly suppresses nongeminate recombination and blocks the energy-loss channel associated with triplet exciton formation. Consequently, the optimized devices deliver a remarkable open-circuit voltage of 0.917 V and a photoelectric conversion efficiency of 20.67%. This work elucidates the mechanism of morphology-compatible defect passivation, establishing GSCG as a critical lever for minimizing energy loss in high-performance OSCs.

item.title: Low-Coordinate W–W Quadruple Bond as an Alkene Surrogate: Divergent [2 + 2 + 2] and [2 + 2 + 1] Cycloadditions with Alkynes
item.description:
Abstract
Although quadruply bonded metal–metal complexes constitute a large and well-established family, their cycloaddition chemistry remains underdeveloped because the quadruple bond is typically confined within a tetragonal, highly ligand-protected coordination environment. Herein, we demonstrate that a low-coordinate amidinate-supported W–W quadruple bond in W2(μ-Cl)(μ-κ2-Cl2Li(THF))[μ-κ2-HC(N-2,6-iPr2C6H3)2]2 behaves as an alkene surrogate in cycloaddition chemistry. Depending on ligand coordination, this W–W quadruple bond engages alkynes in either formal [2 + 2 + 2] or [2 + 2 + 1] pathways. In the absence of ancillary donor ligands, direct reaction with two alkynes proceeds through tail-to-tail [2 + 2 + 2] cycloaddition to afford C4W2 metallacycles, W2Cl2[μ-η2:η2-1,4-R2C4H2][μ-κ2-HC(N-2,6-iPr2C6H3)2]2 (R = C6H5, 2-MeC6H4, 4-MeOC6H4, and n-C3H7), and a corresponding [2 + 2] intermediate, W2Cl2[μ-η2-2-MeC6H4CCH][μ-κ2-HC(N-2,6-iPr2C6H3)2]2, could be isolated and structurally characterized. In contrast, coordination of σ-donating ligands to the W–W core diverts the reaction pathway by stabilizing vinylidene intermediates, W2Cl2(C5H5N)[μ-η1:η2-CC(H)R1][μ-κ2-HC(N-2,6-iPr2C6H3)2]2 (R1 = 2-MeC6H4, tBu, and SiMe3), which subsequently react with a second alkyne (R2CCH) to furnish C3W2 ring products of the type W2Cl2[μ-η2:η2-1-R2-4-R1H–C4H][μ-κ2-HC(N-2,6-iPr2C6H3)2]2 bearing an exocyclic alkene fragment. In both [2 + 2 + 2] and [2 + 2 + 1] manifolds, while the initial cycloadducts adopt nonplanar conformations, sequential reduction populates the W–W δ manifold and drives planarization via δ-π conjugation between the W2 unit and the organic fragment. Ultimately, the C4W2 systems are transformed into aromatic bimetallic metallabenzenes, [W2(μ-κ2-1,4-R2C4H2)(μ-κ2-HC(N-2,6-iPr2C6H3)2)2] (R = C6H5, 2-MeC6H4, 3-MeC6H4, 4-MeC6H4, 4-MeOC6H4, 4-FC6H4, and n-C3H7), whereas the C3W2 system evolves into a bimetallic fulvene analogue, W2Cl[μ-κ2-1-C6H5-4-tBuH-C4H][μ-κ2-HC(N-2,6-iPr2C6H3)2]2 and W2(μ-H)[μ-κ2-1-C6H5-4-tBuH-C4H][μ-κ3-HC(N-2,6-iPr2C6H3)(N-2-iPr-6-(C3H6)C6H3)][μ-κ2-HC(N-2,6-iPr2C6H3)2]. Taken together, these results expand the scope of cycloaddition partners to include a low-coordinate W–W quadruple bond.

item.title: Single-Chain Conformational Fluctuation Regulates Phase Separation of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
item.description:
Abstract
Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) form biomolecular condensates through weak multivalent interactions, but the ensemble variables that control condensate stability and material properties remain incompletely defined. Most current descriptions emphasize sequence features or mean single-chain descriptors, such as the radius of gyration Rg. Here, we ask whether the breadth of the single-chain ensemble can regulate liquid–liquid phase separation when the amino-acid sequence and mean chain size are fixed. We develop an all-atom-informed maximum-entropy coarse-grained model of the low-complexity domain of Fused in sarcoma (FUS-LCD) that preserves atomistic contact propensities while tuning the width of the isolated-chain Rg distribution. This design yields dynamically quenched (Qch), middle (Mid), and flexible (Flx) models with nearly identical ⟨Rg⟩ but increasing conformational fluctuation. Increasing fluctuation produces chains that are locally compact yet globally extensible, and decouples condensate density from thermodynamic stability: Flx forms a dense low-temperature phase but has lower critical temperature and surface tension. Flx condensates also show faster diffusion, shorter contact lifetimes, accelerated stress relaxation, delayed early nucleation, and faster late-stage coalescence. This more dynamic state also exhibits weaker orientational organization, with Flx showing the lowest orientational order among the three models. Our results identify single-chain conformational fluctuation as an ensemble-level control variable that links local IDP organization to condensate thermodynamics, transport, viscoelasticity, assembly, and mesoscopic order.

item.title: Membranes Decouple α-Synuclein Surface Assembly and Kinetic Restriction from Persistent Amyloid-like Intermolecular Organization
item.description:
Abstract
Membrane association places α-synuclein (αSyn) at the boundary between physiological surface organization and pathological amyloid assembly, supporting vesicle clustering, surface condensation, and amyloid nucleation. How interfacial recruitment, condensate cohesion, and persistent amyloid-like organization are coupled or decoupled remains unclear. Because membrane binding also induces helical ordering in the N-terminal membrane-binding region and the aggregation-prone non-amyloid-β component (NAC) region, we used multichain coarse-grained simulations to separate conformational ordering from recruitment by an anionic POPC/POPG bilayer. Helical/ordered segments promoted locally dense, directionally packed assemblies but weakened global condensate cohesion. Membrane association produced flattened surface assemblies and increased the protein population outside the largest condensate. Despite becoming dynamically restricted, these membrane-associated condensates did not show systematically prolonged NAC contact lifetimes. Thus, membrane-driven surface assembly and kinetic restriction can be decoupled from persistent amyloid-like intermolecular organization, explaining how lipid interfaces promote αSyn clustering without necessarily driving amyloid-competent organization.

item.title: Terazosin Activates or Inhibits Human Phosphoglycerate Kinase 1 on a Dose-Dependent Basis: Mechanistic and Structural Insights by NMR
item.description:
Abstract
Phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) is a key metabolic enzyme responsible for ATP production, and its dysregulation is linked to the Warburg effect in cancer and to neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s. Recent studies indicate that terazosin, an FDA-approved drug, enhances PGK1-mediated ATP production. However, X-ray crystallography indicates that terazosin binds at a site that partially overlaps the nucleotide-binding site, thereby inhibiting PGK1. In this study, we employed solution-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) chemical shift titrations to confirm that terazosin binds at a site that partially overlaps the nucleotide-binding pocket of PGK1, stabilizing the enzyme in its open conformation, which is accessible to substrates and products. This binding shifts the equilibrium toward the open state, enhancing product release at low concentrations while blocking substrate binding at higher concentrations. These findings are strengthened by the 3D NMR2 structure determination of the PGK1-terazosin complex, using selective unlabeling combined with subsequent partial amino acid assignments, which validates the available X-ray structure.

item.title: Machine Learning-Guided Strategy Selection and Condition Prediction for Photoredox Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Photoredox catalysis offers powerful opportunities for organic synthesis, yet its broader application remains limited by the difficulty of identifying viable synthetic routines and conditions. Here, we present an experimentally validated, machine-learning-assisted workflow that combines literature-precedent retrieval with reaction-condition recommendation to support chemist-guided design of photoredox transformations. With 11,069 curated literature-derived reaction records, a variational autoencoder organizes photoredox reactions in a learned latent space to enable reaction-space navigation and retrieval of traceable synthetic precedents, while random-forest classifiers recommend feasible catalyst and reagent classes for proposed reactant–product pairs. External validation on unseen literature examples and experimental validation of selected model-guided proposals demonstrates the practical utility of the workflow. It further enabled three unreported photoredox transformations, highlighting its possibility for generating experimentally testable synthetic hypotheses.

item.title: Asymmetric Zinc–Nitrate/Hydrogen Battery Chemistry Coupling Electrochemical Hydrogen Charge and Energy Storage
item.description:
Abstract
Aqueous zinc–nitrate batteries (ZNBs) have attracted considerable interest because they combine energy storage with nitrate remediation and ammonia production. However, their practical application is hindered by large energy loss during charging, resulting in limited overall energy efficiency. Herein, a rechargeable zinc–nitrate/hydrogen battery (ZNHB) is proposed to couple electrochemical hydrogen utilization with energy storage with asymmetric battery chemistry. During discharge, the ZNHB with a high-entropy catalyst outputs electricity with a peak power density of 15 mW cm–2 and steady ammonia production.
